blocks.x: Achala's Data, Analytics & Lakehouse domain turns scattered data estates into decision-grade platforms. Eight practices cover lakehouse architecture, streaming, migration factories and decision products — governed so well that finance signs the numbers without a meeting.

The data domain is the substrate every other domain stands on. Its discipline is contract-first engineering: schemas are versioned agreements with owners, SLAs are typed and monitored, and the layers, bronze, silver, gold, are promotion paths with quality gates rather than folders on a disk.

Seven practices cover the ground: modernization of legacy estates, the lakehouse core itself, streaming for decisions that cannot wait, governance that makes data findable and trustworthy, risk analytics, BI that executives actually use, and monetization for data that leaves the building, where the controls have to be stronger, not looser.

blocks.x: The discipline that separates a data platform from a data swamp is contracts: every pipeline consumes and produces typed agreements with named owners, freshness SLAs and quarantine behavior. When something breaks, the contract tells you who is paged and what downstream is safe, before anyone opens a dashboard to guess.

The economics matter as much as the engineering: storage growth, compute per query and duplicate estates are signed line items, reviewed quarterly with finance. A platform that cannot state its unit cost per workload is not governed; it is merely hosted.

blocks.x: Contracts, not culture — what makes data governed
blocks.sub: Schema contracts, quarantine gates and metric ownership as the mechanics

blocks.x: Data platforms fail culturally when governance means committees and succeed mechanically when it means contracts: every producer signs a schema contract (typed, versioned, owned), every pipeline enforces it at the boundary, and every business metric carries a contract, definition, owner, freshness SLA. The bronze-silver-gold progression is the enforcement spine: bronze is immutable, silver is conformed under quarantine gates, gold is business marts where metric contracts make disputes resolvable by lookup rather than by meeting. Freshness by tier is the console headline, because a platform that cannot say how stale each tier is cannot be trusted by anyone downstream.

The engagement sequence follows the contracts: baseline the estate (sources, consumers, the shadow-spreadsheet census), sign the first producer contracts, deploy the quarantine-and-promotion path, and let the glossary accumulate definitions only as metrics become certified. Release gates demand evidence, a tier without quality SLAs does not carry downstream consumers, a metric without an owner does not reach the board pack.

items: Producer contracts, enforced
Typed and versioned at the boundary; drift breaks the pipeline, not the downstream.
Quarantine as a feature
Failed records are quarantined with reasons, never silently dropped.
Metric contracts on gold
Definition, owner and SLA per metric; disputes resolve by lookup.
Freshness by tier, published
The console tells every consumer exactly how stale each layer is.
We have a warehouse — why a lakehouse?

The warehouse stays useful; the lakehouse adds the governed raw layer and open formats under it. The migration practice prices the dual-run honestly, most estates keep the warehouse serving BI while the lakehouse takes ingest, science and new products.
How do you stop the multiple-versions-of-truth problem?

Metric contracts on the gold layer: one definition, one owner, one freshness SLA per metric. Disputes resolve by lookup instead of meetings, and the dispute rate itself is a console metric we sign against.
What breaks first in a streaming program?

Usually nothing visible, the decisions are simply slower than the events. The streaming practice engineers decision latency as a typed SLA with replay semantics, so late or duplicate events cannot corrupt a decision silently.
Is governance a tool we can install?

The tooling helps; the governance is contracts. Producers sign versioned schemas, pipelines enforce them at the boundary, and every metric carries an owner. Committees do not make data governed; signed agreements do.
Can data products really generate revenue?

Where the controls are stronger, not looser: contract SLAs, entitlement audits and freshness guarantees that external customers can read. The monetization practice starts with the two or three datasets whose commercial value survives those terms.
